artboards.title: A — Calm. Search, the order in progress, then browse.
B — Order-first. The tab IS the order pad.
C — Big targets. Built for glare and one hand.

annotations.text:
WHAT WENT WRONG LAST TIME

I built a shrunken desktop console: 11px uppercase labels, hairline metric strips, dense 56px rows, a navy dashboard widget. That vocabulary is for a manager sitting at a desk working through a complex flow. This is a phone in a yard.

So everything below is new. Same palette and same faces — that part is the brand. Nothing else carried over.

  body text        11-14px  ->  15-16px
  section headings 11px UPPERCASE TRACKED  ->  16px sentence case
  lists            hairline rows  ->  cards on a grey ground
  blocks on Sell   8  ->  3
  borders/shadows  everywhere  ->  none (white on grey is the separation)

PICK A DIRECTION AND I WILL BUILD IT OUT, one screen at a time.

A — CALM

A well-made ordinary app. Search at the top, the one order in progress as a card you can read at arm's length, then a quiet way into the catalogue.

FOR: nothing to learn, and it holds up when there is no order open — the card just isn't there.

AGAINST: the safest of the three. It is a good app, not a memorable one, and building an order still means going somewhere else.

B — ORDER-FIRST

The Sell tab IS the order pad. It opens on what you are building for whoever is standing in front of you. Searching and browsing slide up over it, so the order never leaves the screen.

FOR: the fewest ideas of the three, and it matches the actual job — an agent is always mid-order or about to start one. Send is always in the thumb.

AGAINST: needs a real answer for the first screen a new agent sees, and for switching between two customers in one visit.

C — BIG TARGETS

Six targets, each 100px, and nothing else on the screen. The order rides along the bottom of every screen in the app, always one thumb away.

FOR: works in direct sun, one-handed, with dusty hands. Almost nothing to read.

AGAINST: only six ways in, so search has to be genuinely good; and a full-width oxide bar on every screen spends the accent everywhere.
